Newborn Care

Recognising newborn jaundice and understanding bilirubin tests

Updated: October 7, 2026

Written and edited byMohammadamin Namyar, founder of BeMama: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Noticing yellow skin is a reason to check on your baby, but its shade or spread cannot tell you the bilirubin level. Clinical testing and a clear follow-up plan help distinguish common early jaundice from a problem needing treatment.

What yellow skin can tell you

Newborn jaundice is a yellow appearance caused by a build-up of bilirubin, a substance produced when red blood cells are broken down. It is common in early life, but the visible colour does not show whether a particular baby needs treatment. Timing, feeding, examination and a bilirubin measurement may all matter.

Look at your baby in bright, preferably natural light while keeping them comfortably warm. Yellowing may be visible in the whites of the eyes, inside the mouth or on the skin. Gently pressing the skin briefly can make a change easier to see in the blanched area, but this is a way to notice possible jaundice, not a laboratory test.

Skin pigmentation and lighting can make yellowing harder to recognise. If you are uncertain, ask your midwife or clinician rather than repeatedly checking under different household bulbs. A baby who looks only slightly yellow may still need assessment.

Do not turn the spread of yellowing into a number

Jaundice may appear first around the face and later be noticed elsewhere. That observation cannot reliably assign a bilirubin level to a baby. A chart that equates yellowing of the head, chest, legs or whole body with a particular number of milligrams per decilitre is not a safe home decision tool.

Do not decide that treatment can wait because the legs are not yellow, or that the bilirubin must be above a certain level because the colour seems widespread. Visual assessment is particularly uncertain across different skin tones and under different lighting.

Instead, tell the clinician when you first noticed the change and whether feeding, waking or nappies have changed. If a measurement is needed, the result should be interpreted with the baby’s age and clinical situation. A photograph or comparison with another baby cannot supply that information.

Early jaundice and an unwell baby need rapid help

Jaundice appearing during the first twenty-four hours after birth needs urgent medical assessment and a blood bilirubin test. Do not wait for a routine home visit or for the colour to spread. If your baby is still in hospital, alert staff straight away.

At any age, a jaundiced baby who is difficult to wake, not feeding, unusually floppy or stiff, making abnormal jerking movements, struggling to breathe or clearly unwell needs emergency assessment. An abnormal temperature or absence of wet nappies is also concerning. Use local emergency services if you cannot obtain immediate help safely.

For suspected jaundice after the first day in a baby who otherwise seems well, contact your maternity or newborn care service promptly for advice and testing. Worsening colour or a change in behaviour should prompt another call even if a previous assessment was reassuring.

What a skin bilirubin meter measures

A transcutaneous bilirubin meter is a handheld instrument placed against a suitable area of skin. It uses light to estimate bilirubin without taking a blood sample. BiliChek is one example of a device name, rather than a separate diagnosis or a test that parents need to buy.

A skin reading is an estimate, not a direct measurement of bilirubin in the blood. The professional using it must follow the device instructions and the local clinical pathway. A reassuring-looking display, a particular light colour or a claim of “minimal error” does not replace that interpretation.

Skin markings, bruising, measurement site and circumstances such as recent phototherapy may affect whether the device or reading is suitable. Different instruments do not necessarily operate in exactly the same way. A result may need confirmation with a blood test, especially when it is high or close to a treatment threshold.

When a blood bilirubin test is needed

A serum bilirubin test measures bilirubin in a blood sample. It is used when a skin estimate is unsuitable or needs confirmation. For example, NICE guidance uses serum testing in the first twenty-four hours and for babies born before thirty-five weeks, rather than relying on a skin meter in those situations.

The sample may be collected by a trained professional from a heel prick or another appropriate site. This is not a procedure to attempt at home. Ask how you can comfort your baby during collection, such as holding or feeding when the professional says this is appropriate.

The routine newborn blood-spot screening test and a bilirubin test are not interchangeable just because both may involve a small blood sample. A bilirubin measurement needs the appropriate request, collection and interpretation. Laboratory testing is useful, but sample problems or an unexpected result can still require a repeat test.

Results need the baby’s age and risk factors

There is no single bilirubin number that has the same meaning for every newborn. Clinicians consider age in hours, gestational age at birth, the rate of change and conditions that can increase the risk of bilirubin-related harm. Weight alone is not an adequate basis for deciding whether treatment is needed.

Prematurity and additional risk factors are incorporated into the relevant clinical thresholds. The same result may therefore lead to different plans for two babies of different ages or clinical backgrounds. Do not copy a treatment threshold from another family’s experience or an online discussion.

Ask whether the result is below, near or above the treatment threshold for your baby and when the next check is due. If you are sent home, make sure the follow-up plan includes a time, place and contact route. A single result is a snapshot, not a guarantee that the level will not rise later.

Other tests help explain the cause

Sometimes the clinical team needs more than a bilirubin measurement. Blood groups, a blood count and other investigations may help assess whether red blood cells are being broken down unusually quickly or whether another condition is contributing. The choice depends on the history, examination and pattern of results.

The direct antiglobulin test, often called a DAT or Coombs test, looks for antibodies attached to red blood cells. It can help investigate an immune cause of red-cell breakdown. It does not directly measure bilirubin and is not a replacement for a bilirubin test.

Not every baby automatically needs a DAT or every available investigation. If jaundice is prolonged or there are concerning stool or urine changes, the team may measure the conjugated component of bilirubin and investigate liver or bile-flow problems. Ask what each proposed test is intended to clarify.

Pay attention to stool and urine changes

Pale, chalky or unusually light stools and dark urine that stains the nappy should be reported promptly. They are not routine signs to dismiss as ordinary newborn jaundice. They can point toward a problem with the handling or flow of bile that needs assessment.

Take a clear photograph of an unusual stool or show the nappy if that helps the clinician understand what you have noticed. Do not wait for a planned review weeks later when these changes appear. Equally, normal-looking nappies do not by themselves prove that bilirubin is at a safe level.

Jaundice lasting beyond the expected early period also needs review. NICE identifies persistence beyond fourteen days in babies born at thirty-seven weeks or later, or beyond twenty-one days in babies born earlier, as prolonged jaundice requiring assessment. These time points are not waiting periods for a baby with warning signs.

Home assessment must be part of a clinical service

Some maternity or community services can arrange a professional assessment and, where available, testing at home. This can be helpful when travelling with a newborn is difficult. Availability varies, so a home test should be arranged through the team responsible for your baby’s care.

Ask who will review the result, how quickly you will hear from them and what happens if the level needs treatment. A person arriving with a meter is not enough unless the reading connects to an appropriate assessment and follow-up plan. Do not delay urgent hospital care while waiting for a convenient home appointment.

Concerns about infection exposure, transport or other practical barriers are worth discussing with the service. They should help you choose a safe route to care. They are not a reason to avoid necessary testing or assume that a commercial home service is always the safer choice.

Feeding, treatment and follow-up

Frequent effective feeding supports a newborn’s hydration and bilirubin clearance. If your baby is too sleepy to feed well, feeding is painful or milk transfer is uncertain, ask for help promptly. A feeding count alone cannot prove that intake is adequate, and supporting feeding does not replace a necessary bilirubin check.

Some babies need no specific treatment beyond monitoring and feeding support; others need phototherapy or more intensive care according to their results. Do not use sunlight, sugar water, herbal remedies or ordinary household lamps as substitutes for prescribed treatment. Advice about any additional milk should be individualized by the team.

Before the next check, know which symptoms mean you should return earlier. Keep test results and follow-up details together so the next professional can see the timing and trend. The safest plan combines what you notice at home with clinical assessment rather than asking you to judge severity from colour alone.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Appearance can raise suspicion but cannot quantify bilirubin.

Test results need age in hours, gestational age and clinical risk factors.

First-day jaundice, illness, pale stools or dark urine need timely assessment.

How BeMama can help

Record when yellowing began, feeding and nappy changes, test times and the next appointment. Ask who will call with results and how to get help sooner if your baby changes.

When to seek help

Seek immediate assessment for jaundice in the first day or a jaundiced baby who is hard to wake, feeding poorly, floppy, stiff, breathing abnormally or acutely unwell. Report pale stools or dark urine promptly.

Evidence notes updated: October 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Do not estimate a bilirubin number from skin colour.
  • A skin meter gives an estimate; some babies need blood testing.
  • A Coombs test investigates a possible cause, not the bilirubin level itself.
  • Pale stools and dark urine should not be dismissed.
  • Home testing needs a professional result and follow-up pathway.

Frequently asked questions

Can the spread of yellow skin tell me the bilirubin number?

No. Visual spread cannot reliably assign a bilirubin level or determine whether treatment is needed.

Does a baby with darker skin still need a jaundice check?

Yes. Yellowing may be harder to notice, so uncertainty or concerning symptoms should prompt professional assessment.

Can I wait for tomorrow’s visit if jaundice begins on the first day?

No. Jaundice within twenty-four hours needs urgent assessment and a blood bilirubin test.

Does a skin meter directly measure bilirubin in blood?

No. It estimates bilirubin through the skin and may need confirmation with a blood sample.

Is BiliChek something I should buy to manage jaundice myself?

No. It is a device used within a clinical testing pathway, not a substitute for newborn assessment.

Is the routine newborn blood-spot screen also a bilirubin test?

No. A bilirubin test requires its own appropriate request and interpretation.

Does a Coombs test replace a bilirubin measurement?

No. It looks for antibodies attached to red blood cells and can help investigate a cause of jaundice.

Are pale stools and dark urine ordinary harmless jaundice signs?

No. Report them promptly because they can indicate a liver or bile-flow problem.

Can a home test mean we do not need follow-up?

No. The result must be reviewed with the baby’s age and condition, and further checks or treatment may be needed.

Can I treat jaundice by putting the baby in sunlight?

No. Sunlight is not a substitute for prescribed phototherapy or clinical assessment.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
